prompt: A developer changes shared_buffers on production because a blog post recommended it. Which way did the line between roles get crossed?

choices.text: An administrator acted above the line
choices.why: Nobody administering acted here.

choices.text: A developer acted below the line
choices.why: Right. Server configuration is the administrator's.

choices.text: It is on the shared layer, the schema
choices.why: shared_buffers is not schema.

choices.text: No line was crossed: settings are everyone's
choices.why: Server settings sit below the line.

prompt: What is the first day with an inherited server for, according to the course?

choices.text: Applying the pending minor upgrades
choices.why: That is a change, and changes come from the inventory.

choices.text: An inventory, written down and dated
choices.why: Right. Nothing is fixed yet.

choices.text: Resetting the settings nobody can explain
choices.why: Such a setting may be holding something up.

choices.text: Moving the server to a managed service
choices.why: That is a project, not a first day.

prompt: Which of these questions belong to the administrator's five? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Can it be restored?
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Will it still fit?
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Is the query well written?
choices.why: That is the developer's question.

choices.text: Who can do what?
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Which framework does the application use?
choices.why: Not a question about the server.

prompt: A team asks for a new database on an Oracle server for a new service. What will most likely be created?

choices.text: A new cluster with its own data directory
choices.why: That is PostgreSQL's vocabulary, and far more than asked.

choices.text: A new user, which brings its own schema
choices.why: Right. In Oracle, schema and user are one thing.

choices.text: A new login on the instance
choices.why: That is SQL Server's split.

choices.text: A new binary log
choices.why: That is MySQL's replication log.

prompt: Match each engine to the name of its change log.
Why does PostgreSQL show one line per connection in ps while MySQL does not?

choices.text: MySQL refuses connections over the socket
choices.why: It accepted sudo mysql over the socket.

choices.text: PostgreSQL uses processes, MySQL threads
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: ps hides programs run by the user mysql
choices.why: mysqld appeared in the same ps.

choices.text: PostgreSQL starts a process per query
choices.why: Per connection.

prompt: Why does the course recommend a virtual machine rather than the laptop you work on?

choices.text: PostgreSQL needs a hypervisor to run
choices.why: It runs on any Linux.

choices.text: Virtual machines run databases faster
choices.why: If anything slightly slower.

choices.text: Ubuntu only allows PostgreSQL in a VM
choices.why: Any Ubuntu installs it.

choices.text: You break it on purpose, away from your files
choices.why: Right.

prompt: On a fresh Ubuntu install, `psql` says `role "ana" does not exist`. What is the fix?

choices.text: sudo systemctl restart postgresql
choices.why: The server is running; it just does not know you.

choices.text: psql -U postgres
choices.why: Peer authentication refuses it.

choices.text: sudo -u postgres createuser --superuser $USER
choices.why: Right; then createdb $USER.

choices.text: sudo apt install --reinstall postgresql
choices.why: Nothing is missing from the installation.

prompt: Which of these is a managed service most likely to refuse your role?

choices.text: Reading a file on the server
choices.why: Right. Anything that reaches the operating system.

choices.text: Creating a schema
choices.why: Inside the database you have wide powers.

choices.text: Granting SELECT to another role
choices.why: Grants are yours.

choices.text: Running VACUUM on a table
choices.why: Maintenance inside the database is allowed.

prompt: A connection over the local socket is allowed only for the role named like the operating-system user. That rule is called ___ authentication.
You move a container from postgres:16 to postgres:17 and keep its volume. What happens?

choices.text: It refuses to start on version 16's files
choices.why: Right. Lesson 20 is about moving the data.

choices.text: The server upgrades the data on its first start
choices.why: No server converts another major version's files by itself.

choices.text: Docker refuses to mount the volume
choices.why: Docker mounts it; PostgreSQL refuses.

choices.text: Both versions share the files safely
choices.why: The format differs between major versions.

prompt: Order the steps from a fresh Ubuntu server to a psql prompt of your own.
Where does Ubuntu keep postgresql.conf for the cluster 16/main?

choices.text: /etc/postgresql/16/main
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: /var/lib/postgresql/16/main

choices.text: /var/log/postgresql
choices.why: That holds the log.

choices.text: /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin
choices.why: That holds the programs.

choices.text: Dead rows

choices.text: The write-ahead log of the load
choices.why: WAL is not counted in any relation's size.

choices.text: The indexes, and the free space and visibility maps

choices.text: A copy kept for crash recovery
choices.why: No such copy exists.

prompt: A table's main fork is 3.2 GB and segment_size is 1GB. How many files hold it?
After `TRUNCATE orders`, a script that remembered the path base/16386/16398 finds the file gone. Why?

choices.text: TRUNCATE moved the table to another tablespace
choices.why: It moves nothing.

choices.text: TRUNCATE gave the table a new file

choices.text: Autovacuum deletes empty files
choices.why: The file was replaced by TRUNCATE itself.

choices.text: The database got a new oid
choices.why: Nothing happened to the database.

prompt: The disk is nearly full and pg_wal is large. Which action does the course rule out?

choices.text: Finding out why pg_wal grew
choices.why: That is the first step.

choices.text: Reading the server's log
choices.why: Always a good step.

choices.text: Deleting old files in pg_wal by hand
choices.why: Right. The cluster may never start again.

choices.text: Measuring each directory with du
choices.why: Measuring changes nothing.

prompt: What does `sudo pg_dropcluster --stop 16 main` remove?

choices.text: The data directory only
choices.why: It also removes the configuration and the log.

choices.text: The postgresql-16 package
choices.why: The programs stay.

choices.text: Its data, its configuration and its log
choices.why: Right. Nothing asks twice.

choices.text: Every cluster on the machine
choices.why: Only the one named.

prompt: Why is a tablespace on a separate disk a risk for backups?

choices.text: It is part of the cluster yet lives outside the data directory
choices.why: Right. A tool has to follow the link, and a restore has to recreate it.

choices.text: Tablespaces cannot hold indexes
choices.why: They can.

choices.text: The server stops writing WAL for it
choices.why: Its changes go through the WAL like any other.

choices.text: Only superusers may back it up
choices.why: That is not the issue.

prompt: The file in the data directory that exists only while the server runs, and records its process id, is postmaster.___.
Match each fork to what it holds.
`ALTER DATABASE shop SET work_mem = '16MB'` and `ALTER ROLE app SET work_mem = '32MB'` are both in place. The role app opens a connection to shop. Which work_mem does the session start with?

choices.text: 16MB, because the database is read last
choices.why: The role's layer outranks the database's.

choices.text: 4MB, the compiled default, until a reload
choices.why: Both values apply when a connection starts; no reload is involved.

choices.text: 32MB
choices.why: Right. Where a role and a database both set a value, the role's wins.

choices.text: Whichever ALTER ran most recently
choices.why: The order is fixed by layer, not by time.

prompt: `log_min_duration_statement = 250ms` is the only line that sets it, in a conf.d file. Somebody puts a `#` in front of it and runs a reload. What value is in force afterwards?

choices.text: Still 250ms until the next restart
choices.why: It is a sighup parameter; a reload applies the change.

choices.text: Whatever value the commented line itself shows
choices.why: A comment is not read as a setting.

choices.text: None: the reload fails on the commented line
choices.why: A comment is valid syntax.

choices.text: -1, the compiled default, as no line sets it now
choices.why: Right. The line is gone, so the default applies; the comment's text plays no part.

prompt: After the restart, `pg_settings` showed `shared_buffers` with setting 32768 and unit 8kB. How many megabytes is that?
A conf.d file was edited and `systemctl reload` printed nothing. Where does a bad line in the file show itself? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The server's log
choices.why: Yes: the reload's lines name the parameter and the file.

choices.text: The error column of pg_file_settings
choices.why: Yes: it reads the files as they are on disk.

choices.text: postgres -C with the config_file, run as postgres
choices.why: Yes: it reads every file and prints the FATAL a restart would die on.

choices.text: The exit status of systemctl reload
choices.why: It succeeded: it only delivers a signal.

choices.text: The pg_hba_file_rules view
choices.why: That view reads pg_hba.conf, not the parameter files.

prompt: Following the course's budget, what effective_cache_size suits a dedicated server with 8 GB of memory?

choices.text: 2GB, the same quarter as shared_buffers
choices.why: That is the shared cache alone; the page cache counts too.

choices.text: 8GB, the whole of the machine
choices.why: The system and the processes take part of it.

choices.text: 6GB
choices.why: Right: about three quarters of the machine, and it allocates nothing.

choices.text: 1GB at most, or the machine runs out of memory
choices.why: It allocates nothing, so its value exhausts no memory.

prompt: With shared_buffers at 128 MB, a 20 MB table is read in full by a sequential scan, then read again. What does the second scan's Buffers line show?

choices.text: read again, apart from a ring of 32 buffers per process
choices.why: The ring is for a table larger than a quarter of shared_buffers, 32 MB here.

choices.text: read, since a sequential scan bypasses the cache
choices.why: Every read goes through shared_buffers.

choices.text: hit for nearly all of its pages
choices.why: Right. Under a quarter of the cache, the scan uses ordinary buffers and the pages stay.

choices.text: No line: the planner's statistics answer it
choices.why: Statistics describe a table; they hold no rows.

prompt: By the course's count, how many megabytes may a query with one hash join and two sorts use at most, run in a single process with no parallel helpers and work_mem = 32MB?
Match each Sort Method in EXPLAIN ANALYZE to what it says about the sort.

pairs.right: it kept only the first rows

right_distractors: it read its pages from the page cache

prompt: Seconds after a commit, a colleague greps the table's file for the new row's text, finds nothing, and says the commit was lost. What is actually true?

choices.text: It was lost and has to be repeated
choices.why: COMMIT returned, so its record had reached the disk in the log.

choices.text: The row went to a temporary file in base/pgsql_tmp
choices.why: Those files hold spilled sorts, not committed rows.

choices.text: The row is in a WAL segment and in a dirty page in memory
choices.why: Right. The table file catches up at the next checkpoint.

choices.text: grep cannot read the file while the server runs
choices.why: It read it with sudo and counted 0 matches.

prompt: A server was built with wal_level = minimal. Next month the team wants a standby copying it. What has to happen on the primary first?

choices.text: wal_level = replica, and a reload
choices.why: Changing wal_level needs a restart, not a reload.

choices.text: archive_mode = on, keeping wal_level as it is
choices.why: No archive and no replica can be built from minimal.

choices.text: Nothing: max_wal_senders is already 10
choices.why: Room to stream does not make the records carry enough.

choices.text: wal_level = replica, and a restart
choices.why: Right. minimal records too little for a replica, and the setting is read at start.

prompt: Right after a checkpoint, updating every row of the 66 MB orders_copy wrote 234 MB of WAL, and the identical second pass wrote 171 MB. How many megabytes more did the first pass write?
Match each value of wal_level to what the log records.

pairs.right: enough for recovery, replicas and archives
that, plus what decoding needs to rebuild rows

right_distractors: nothing: the log is switched off

prompt: The same 40,000 pgbench transactions took 59334 full-page images with max_wal_size = 64MB and 27489 at the default. How many more images did the frequent checkpoints cause?
The server is stopped with `systemctl stop` and started again a minute later. What does this start leave out that a start after kill -9 does?

choices.text: Reading global/pg_control
choices.why: Every start reads it first; that is how it knows the stop was clean.

choices.text: Opening the socket and the TCP port to clients
choices.why: Both starts listen; those lines open every start.

choices.text: Checking each data file's pages with amcheck
choices.why: No start runs amcheck.

choices.text: Replaying the log from the redo point
choices.why: Right. pg_control says shut down, so no automatic recovery runs.

prompt: In which of these cases is fsync = off defensible, by the lesson's account?

choices.text: A primary whose crashes so far were all kill -9
choices.why: A kill -9 cannot show the damage; a power cut can.

choices.text: A server where losing the last second of commits is acceptable
choices.why: That is synchronous_commit = off, which keeps the database consistent.

choices.text: A primary on ext4 with full_page_writes on
choices.why: full_page_writes does not restore the order fsync enforces.

choices.text: A first load into a copy you will discard if it fails
choices.why: Right. It is a database you are prepared to throw away and build again.

prompt: Put what one checkpoint does in order.
items: note the redo point, where the log is now
write every dirty page to its file
force those files onto the disk
write the checkpoint record into the log
recycle or remove the segments older than the redo point
trap: The record comes last among the writes: a change made while the pages were written may not be in its file, which is why recovery starts from the redo point.

prompt: A cluster upgraded from PostgreSQL 13 now runs 16 with password_encryption = scram-sha-256. Which roles still have an md5 value stored?

choices.text: None: the upgrade converts each stored password
choices.why: A verifier cannot be computed from an md5 value; a new password replaces it.

choices.text: The superusers
choices.why: Being a superuser has nothing to do with how a password is stored.

choices.text: Every role, until the server is restarted
choices.why: A restart changes no stored password.

choices.text: Those whose password nobody has set since
choices.why: Right. An md5 value stays until that password is set again.

prompt: A team lead, not a superuser, has to decide who joins reporting and who leaves it. Which grant gives her exactly that?

choices.text: ALTER ROLE lead CREATEROLE
choices.why: On 16 that creates roles, and manages the ones it holds ADMIN on.

choices.text: GRANT reporting TO lead WITH INHERIT TRUE, SET TRUE
choices.why: Those let her use and become the group, not hand it out.

choices.text: GRANT reporting TO lead WITH ADMIN TRUE
choices.why: Right. ADMIN lets a member grant the group to others and revoke it.

choices.text: GRANT pg_signal_backend TO lead
choices.why: That role stops sessions; it grants no memberships.

prompt: In pg_authid, the start of a password set on PostgreSQL 16 read `SCRAM-SHA-256$N`. How many rounds of hashing is N?
libpq reads passwords for programs from a file in the home directory, ~/.___, and ignores it when other users have read access.
A view in reports is created WITH (security_invoker = true) over orders. reporting has USAGE on reports and SELECT on the view, and nothing on orders. What does bruno's query on the view get?

choices.text: The rows, read with the view owner's privileges
choices.why: That is an ordinary view; security_invoker turns it off.

choices.text: permission denied for schema reports
choices.why: USAGE on reports was granted; the schema door is open.

choices.text: Zero rows and no error
choices.why: That is row-level security with no policy, not a missing privilege.

choices.text: permission denied for table orders
choices.why: Right. Such a view checks the querying role's privileges on the tables beneath it.

prompt: app holds UPDATE (status) and SELECT (id) on orders, and nothing else on it. Which statement succeeds?

choices.text: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 7
choices.why: Right. The WHERE reads only id, and app holds SELECT on id.

choices.text: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE customer_id = 5
choices.why: The WHERE reads customer_id, and app has no SELECT on it.

choices.text: UPDATE orders SET status = upper(status) WHERE id = 7
choices.why: The right-hand side reads status, which needs SELECT on it.

choices.text: UPDATE orders SET total_cents = 0 WHERE id = 7
choices.why: app's UPDATE grant covers status alone.

prompt: Row-level security is enabled on customers, without FORCE, and a policy shows reporting only Brazilian rows. Who reads all 50,000 rows? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A superuser
choices.why: Yes: a superuser skips the policies.

choices.text: A role with BYPASSRLS
choices.why: Yes: that attribute exists for exactly this, a backup's role above all.

choices.text: The table's owner
choices.why: Yes, unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set on the table.

choices.text: bruno, through reporting's column grants
choices.why: Grants decide the columns; the policy still filters his rows.

choices.text: A role with SELECT on the table and no policy for it
choices.why: With no policy for it, it sees zero rows.

prompt: An ordinary view runs its query with the privileges of the view's ___, which is how bruno reads a sum over orders with no grant on orders.
A monitoring tool tried out as a superuser showed every query. Deployed as its own role monitor, it lists sessions with `<insufficient privilege>` instead. What is the narrowest fix?

choices.text: ALTER ROLE monitor SUPERUSER
choices.why: It works, and it hands a monitoring agent the absence of every check.

choices.text: GRANT pg_monitor TO monitor
choices.why: Right. It shows every session's query and the statistics a tool reads.

choices.text: GRANT pg_read_all_data TO monitor
choices.why: That reads tables, not other sessions' activity.

choices.text: GRANT pg_signal_backend TO monitor
choices.why: That stops sessions; it does not show their queries.

prompt: After `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE shop_owner REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC`, a migration running as shop_owner creates a function. app calls it. What happens?

choices.text: It is refused until somebody grants EXECUTE to app
choices.why: Right. Only the owner keeps X on the functions shop_owner creates.

choices.text: It runs: PUBLIC holds EXECUTE on each new function
choices.why: That built-in default is what the statement removed.

choices.text: It runs, because app has CONNECT on shop
choices.why: CONNECT is the first door, not a right on a function.

choices.text: It runs for functions in the public schema alone
choices.why: The row has no schema, so it applies in every schema of shop.

prompt: Which predefined roles should be granted as rarely as SUPERUSER, because they amount to one? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: pg_read_server_files
choices.why: Yes: it reads files on the server as postgres.

choices.text: pg_write_server_files
choices.why: Yes: writing the server's files can rewrite its configuration.

choices.text: pg_execute_server_program
choices.why: Yes: it runs programs on the server as the postgres user.

choices.text: pg_read_all_data
choices.why: It reads tables, and row-level security still filters it.

choices.text: pg_monitor
choices.why: It sees sessions and statistics, not files.

prompt: A default privilege is applied to an object at the moment it is ___, which is why an ALTER TABLE ... OWNER TO afterwards adds no grant.
Right after pg_restore, with no statistics at all, how many rows does the planner expect `status = 'cancelled'` to match in a table of 2,000,000 rows?
A server goes from 16.2 to 16.15 with apt and a restart. What does that do to the planner's statistics?

choices.text: They are lost, so vacuumdb --analyze-in-stages has to run
choices.why: That is after a restore, or after pg_upgrade up to version 17.

choices.text: Nothing: pg_statistic stays with the data directory
choices.why: Right. A minor upgrade replaces the programs and keeps the data, statistics included.

choices.text: They fall back to the half-percent guess until autovacuum
choices.why: That guess is for a table with no statistics at all.

choices.text: The counters in pg_stat_user_tables start from zero
choices.why: Those are written to disk at a clean shutdown; a crash is what zeroes them.

prompt: ANALYZE of a 50-million-row table takes about as long as ANALYZE of a 1-million-row one, at the default target. Why?

choices.text: Each one reads a sample of 30,000 rows, whatever the size
choices.why: Right: 300 rows per unit of the target, which is 100.

choices.text: The bigger table is read from the page cache
choices.why: Neither table is read in full.

choices.text: ANALYZE skips tables above ten million rows
choices.why: It analyses tables of any size, from a sample.

choices.text: Autovacuum has already done half the work
choices.why: A manual ANALYZE starts from scratch; it shares no work.

prompt: After a restore, `vacuumdb --analyze-in-___ -d shop` gives every table rough statistics at once and the full ones behind them.

After an operating-system upgrade the collation warning appears. ana runs ALTER DATABASE shop REFRESH COLLATION VERSION today and plans REINDEX DATABASE for Saturday. What is the state until Saturday?

choices.text: Safe: the refresh rebuilt the text indexes
choices.why: It records a version; it rebuilds nothing.

choices.text: The database refuses connections until the REINDEX
choices.why: A mismatch is a WARNING; connections go on.

choices.text: Queries on text columns fail with an error
choices.why: They give wrong answers with no error, which is the danger.

choices.text: Indexes in the old order, and no warning left to say so
choices.why: Right. Refreshing first only silences the warning.

prompt: A plain `REINDEX INDEX orders_created_at` holds its locks inside an open transaction. Which of these runs without waiting?

choices.text: SELECT name, country FROM customers WHERE country = 'BR'
choices.why: Right. The REINDEX locks orders and that index, nothing else.

choices.text: SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = 1
choices.why: Planning it opens every index of orders, the one being rebuilt included.

choices.text: UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 1
choices.why: A write conflicts with the ShareLock on orders.

choices.text: INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at) VALUES (1, 'paid', 990, now())
choices.why: An insert is a write, and waits like the update.

prompt: Which check of the indexes of orders can run at noon on a busy primary without blocking a single write?

choices.text: bt_index_parent_check
choices.why: It checks more, and takes a lock that blocks writes.

choices.text: bt_index_check with heapallindexed => true
choices.why: Right. It takes only the lock a SELECT takes.

choices.text: REINDEX TABLE orders, which also proves the indexes sound
choices.why: It holds ShareLock, and every write waits for it.

choices.text: A plain CREATE INDEX of a spare copy to compare with
choices.why: A plain CREATE INDEX takes ShareLock and blocks writes too.

prompt: In pg_stat_activity, a REINDEX CONCURRENTLY waiting for an older transaction to end shows wait_event_type Lock and wait_event ___.
pg_stat_statements has collected a week of counts. The server then crashes and recovers. What is left of the counts?

choices.text: All of them, replayed from the WAL
choices.why: The counts live in shared memory, not in any table the log describes.

choices.text: The counts up to the last checkpoint
choices.why: A checkpoint writes pages, not these counts.

choices.text: Nothing: they start again from zero
choices.why: Right. A clean shutdown writes them to disk; a crash loses them.

choices.text: The 5000 most used statements, the rest forgotten
choices.why: pg_stat_statements.max limits what it keeps while running; a crash loses everything.

prompt: apt has just replaced pgcrypto.so with a newer build, and the server was not restarted. Which sessions run the new library?

choices.text: None, until ALTER EXTENSION pgcrypto UPDATE
choices.why: That updates the SQL objects; the .so is loaded fresh by the next backend that needs it.

choices.text: Backends that load it from now on, at their first pgcrypto call
choices.why: Right. A library is loaded into a backend when first needed and stays until that connection ends.

choices.text: Every session at once, including those that already called it
choices.why: A backend keeps what it loaded until its connection ends.

choices.text: None until a restart, as with every library
choices.why: A restart is for libraries in shared_preload_libraries; pgcrypto is not one.

prompt: Two users pick the same password, and each is stored with crypt(password, gen_salt('bf')). What do the two stored values look like?

choices.text: Different, each with its own salt inside
choices.why: Right. That is the difference from digest, which gives both the same value.

choices.text: Identical, as with a SHA-256 digest
choices.why: The random salt makes them differ.

choices.text: Identical in the cost and the hash, apart from the email
choices.why: The 22 characters of salt differ, and so does the hash after them.

choices.text: The password in plain text, since crypt is reversible
choices.why: Nothing in the column decodes back into a password.

prompt: On a geography column, ST_Distance and ST_DWithin measure along the surface of the Earth, in ___.
The same 10,000 pgbench transactions grew the log by 8758557 bytes with log_statement = 'all' and by 10159212 bytes with log_min_duration_statement = 0. How many bytes more did the second cost?
On a server with the default logging settings, autovacuum spends three minutes on a large table. What does that run leave in the log?

choices.text: A line with its duration, as for any slow statement
choices.why: log_min_duration_statement is off by default, and autovacuum has its own threshold.

choices.text: No line at all
choices.why: Right. log_autovacuum_min_duration is 600000 ms: only runs over ten minutes are logged.

choices.text: A WARNING, since it ran longer than a minute
choices.why: A long autovacuum run is not a warning.

choices.text: A checkpoint line saying it started because of autovacuum
choices.why: A checkpoint starts for time, wal or a command.

prompt: A server is moved to logging_collector = on and log_destination = 'jsonlog', with the other settings left alone. Six months later, what has been deleting the old log files?

choices.text: logrotate, which keeps ten weeks of them
choices.why: logrotate watches /var/log/postgresql; the files are in the data directory now.

choices.text: The server, which keeps ten files
choices.why: That is logrotate's rotate 10, for the other arrangement.

choices.text: systemd's journal, which takes them over
choices.why: The journal held only the unit's start and stop.

choices.text: Nothing: the server rotates them by age and size, and keeps them all
choices.why: Right. Old files go only with log_truncate_on_rotation and a repeating log_filename, or something outside the server.

prompt: With log_connections on, the `connection authenticated` line names the method, and the file and line number of ___ whose rule matched.

A MySQL report builds names with CONCAT(first_name, ' ', middle_name, ' ', last_name), and shows NULL for people with no middle name. After the move, the same expression runs with PostgreSQL's concat. What do those people get?

choices.text: Their names, with the NULL skipped
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL's concat skips NULL; its || would return NULL.

choices.text: NULL, exactly as in MySQL
choices.why: Same name, different function.

choices.text: An error: concat does not exist in PostgreSQL
choices.why: concat exists; IFNULL is the one that does not.

choices.text: An empty string for the whole name
choices.why: The other parts are still there.

prompt: A MySQL column is BIGINT UNSIGNED and holds values close to its maximum. What type does it need in PostgreSQL?

choices.text: bigint
choices.why: bigint holds half the unsigned range.

choices.text: integer
choices.why: Narrower still.

choices.text: numeric(20)
choices.why: Right. No signed integer type is wide enough.

choices.text: bigint with a CHECK (value >= 0)
choices.why: The check forbids negatives; it does not widen the type.

prompt: After the pgloader migration, a reporting tool that sets its own search_path to public cannot find customers, while psql can. Why?

choices.text: pgloader kept the name as "Customers", with a capital
choices.why: It folded every name to lower case.

choices.text: The tables sit in a schema named legacy, which the database's own path adds
choices.why: Right. pgloader set the database's search_path to public, legacy; the tool's own setting replaces it.

choices.text: The tool's role has no CONNECT on legacy
choices.why: Without CONNECT it would not have logged in to look.

choices.text: pgloader wrote the tables into the database postgres
choices.why: It wrote into the target database, legacy.

prompt: MySQL's `LIMIT 2, 1` is written in PostgreSQL as `LIMIT 1 ___ 2`, a form both engines accept.
A column is varchar(40) on a 300-million-row table, and somebody proposes ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE varchar(20). How does that compare with going from varchar(20) to varchar(40)?

choices.text: The same: a catalogue edit in milliseconds
choices.why: Raising the limit is the catalogue-only direction.

choices.text: Far costlier: each row is checked under the lock
choices.why: Right. Lowering a limit has to look at every row; raising one invalidates none.

choices.text: Cheaper, since the column gets smaller
choices.why: Smaller is what forces the check.

choices.text: Refused: a varchar limit is fixed when the table is created
choices.why: Both directions are allowed; they differ in cost.

prompt: An unused column must go from a two-billion-row table. For how long does ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN hold the table closed?

choices.text: As long as it takes to read and rewrite each of the two billion rows
choices.why: Dropping a column rewrites nothing.

choices.text: Until VACUUM FULL has run on it
choices.why: No VACUUM is part of a DROP COLUMN.

choices.text: As long as a backfill in batches takes
choices.why: A backfill fills a new column; dropping needs none.

choices.text: A moment: it is marked dropped in the catalogue
choices.why: Right. The bytes stay in the rows until they are next rewritten.

prompt: An index built with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY becomes the primary key in a moment with `ALTER TABLE orders_live ADD CONSTRAINT orders_live_pkey PRIMARY KEY ___ INDEX orders_live_id`.
Match each statement on orders_live to the lock it takes on the table, as the lesson's captures showed.

pairs.left: ALTER TABLE orders_live ADD COLUMN note text
ALTER TABLE orders_live VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_positive
SELECT count(*) FROM orders_live, in an open transaction

prompt: Two reloads. In one, a conf.d file has a valid line and `work_mem = 64mb`. In the other, a file has a valid line and the misspelt `log_min_duraton_statement`. In which did the valid line take effect?

choices.text: The first: a bad value spares the rest, an unknown name refuses the file
choices.why: Right. The two logs said 'unaffected changes were applied' and 'no changes were applied'.

choices.text: Both: the server applies each line it understands
choices.why: An unrecognised parameter got the whole file refused.

choices.text: Neither: any error refuses the file whole
choices.why: A bad value left the other changes applied.

choices.text: The second: names are checked later than values
choices.why: It went the other way round.

prompt: settings.sql leaves out cluster_name, port and external_pid_file by name. Why those three?

choices.text: Their source is default, which the WHERE already drops
choices.why: Then naming them would be pointless; they come from the configuration.

choices.text: psql sets them for its own connection
choices.why: That is the source client, dropped separately.

choices.text: Two clusters must differ in them, so a difference is not drift
choices.why: Right. Each cluster has its own: staging answered on 5433 beside main's 5432.

choices.text: They are hidden from roles below superuser
choices.why: Any role reads them.

prompt: At 3 a.m. work_mem was fixed with ALTER SYSTEM. Put the steps that keep the fix from becoming drift in order.
items: ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem and a reload, during the incident
commit the value to 50-shop.conf with the reason
run provision.sh, which copies the file and reloads
ALTER SYSTEM RESET work_mem, and a reload
check that work_mem's sourcefile in pg_settings is 50-shop.conf
trap: Resetting before the file carries the value would drop the server back to the old number in the middle of the night's fix.

prompt: On a managed service, `terraform ___` compares what the files say with what the provider reports and lists every difference before changing anything.
You are writing a runbook for 'too many connections'. Which line belongs under Check?

choices.text: psql -c "SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;"
choices.why: Right. It only reads, so anybody runs it at any time.

choices.text: psql -c "SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle';"
choices.why: It ends sessions: that is an act, with a finding to name.

choices.text: psql -c "ALTER SYSTEM SET max_connections = 300;"
choices.why: It changes the server, so it is an act, and it needs a restart.

choices.text: sudo systemctl restart postgresql
choices.why: A restart cuts every connection; it is the opposite of a check.

prompt: max_slot_wal_keep_size is set, and a replica stays switched off until its slot holds more than that. What happens?

choices.text: The server stops accepting writes until the replica returns
choices.why: Writes go on; the slot is what is given up.

choices.text: wal_status becomes lost, and the disk stops filling
choices.why: Right. The server gives up on the slot; the replica cannot continue from it and has to be rebuilt.

choices.text: wal_status turns extended and the slot keeps holding
choices.why: extended is past max_wal_size; past this limit the slot is given up.

choices.text: The slot is dropped and made again at the current position
choices.why: Nothing makes it again; its wal_status shows lost.

prompt: Check 3 has just found an inactive slot retaining WAL. Put the rest of the runbook's path in order.
items: ask the slot's owner whether a replica still uses it
note who answered, and what they said
verify: the slot is gone and df stops climbing
trap: The drop cannot be undone, which is why the question and its answer come before it.

prompt: On a night like the lesson's, the inactive slot holds 3 GB and max_wal_size is 1GB. After the slot is dropped and CHECKPOINT runs, what does pg_wal do?

choices.text: Stays at 3 GB until the server is restarted
choices.why: The checkpoint removes what is beyond max_wal_size; no restart is needed.

choices.text: Empties completely, giving back all 3 GB at once
choices.why: Files under max_wal_size are recycled, not removed.

choices.text: Loses what lies beyond 1GB, and recycles the rest
choices.why: Right. Files under max_wal_size are kept for reuse; the WAL beyond it is removed.

choices.text: Keeps growing, as the slot's WAL is now orphaned
choices.why: Nothing holds WAL any more, so it stops growing.
